questions.q: Why can't a single-run comparison with no reported variance support a strong claim about which method is better?
options: Single runs are always fabricated
The entire reported gap might fall within normal seed-to-seed noise
Single runs are illegal to publish
Variance only matters for computer vision tasks
questions.explain: Neural network training is stochastic, so without multiple seeds and reported variance, a reported improvement could simply be within the normal range of run-to-run noise.

Reporting only the best run from an undisclosed sweep as if it were a single clean result
Running out of GPU memory during a sweep
A dataset version mismatch
questions.explain: When only the best-performing run from a sweep is reported without disclosing that a sweep occurred, the resulting number is optimistic compared to what a single clean run would typically achieve.

questions.q: Why are Papers With Code-style leaderboards useful for spotting a baseline tuning gap?
options: They automatically re-run every baseline for you
They let you cross-check a paper's reported baseline number against other papers' reported numbers for that same baseline
They only list the newest methods
They remove the need to read the paper at all
questions.explain: If a paper's baseline number is unusually low compared to how that same baseline performs in other papers, it's a signal the baseline may have been under-tuned.

questions.q: What does 'dataset version and split drift' refer to?
options: Datasets becoming corrupted during download
A dataset's version, split definitions, or labels changing over time, making 'the same dataset' not actually the same data
Datasets being deleted from public repositories
A change in file format only, with no effect on results
questions.explain: Datasets get revised, rebalanced, or corrected over time, and benchmark splits can change between library versions, so recording the exact version and split used is necessary for a fair comparison.

questions.q: Why might a reproduction attempt on different hardware produce different numbers even with identical logical hyperparameters?
options: Hardware never affects numerical results
Factors like numerical precision (fp32 vs. fp16/bf16) and hardware-specific kernels can shift outcomes even when the stated hyperparameters match
Different hardware always runs the exact same code path with no variation
Only consumer GPUs produce inconsistent results
questions.explain: Precision settings and hardware-specific kernel implementations can introduce numerical differences that aren't captured by the hyperparameters listed in a paper.
